source.title: Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification through Scale
source.authors: Soham De; Leonard Berrada; Jamie Hayes; Samuel L. Smith; Borja Balle

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly measures train–validation gaps while varying batch size and reports that the gap increases with batch size, qualifying the claim that larger batches generally improve generalization. Its experiments use DP-SGD, not the standard non-private training setting of the claim.
record.gate_note: Rows report the paper’s own train/validation accuracy comparisons and its explicit statement about the gap. Results cited from earlier work and values available only in figures without a textual result description are omitted.
record.test_reason: The authors report their own finding that dropout reduced training and validation accuracy in private CIFAR-10 classifiers, bearing on V6 in a new training setting. The batch-size experiments do not hold epochs fixed and therefore do not test V5's large-batch penalty. A growing training–validation gap is not evidence of worse held-out accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's statements about batch size, compute and removing regularizers are accurate but omit the main conclusion: scaling models, computational budgets and public pre-training data substantially narrows the accuracy gap between private and non-private image classification using standard architectures with modest modifications.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains with differentially private SGD on image classification, while the claim concerns ordinary gradient training, memorization of random labels, and non-private generalization. The paper studies batch size and regularization only within its DP-SGD experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: On CIFAR-10 under DP-SGD, the training–validation gap increases with batch size. The optimal epoch budget increases with batch size for large batches. Dropout and weight decay are omitted in the paper’s private training pipelines; the authors state they reduced both training and validation accuracy when used.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches improve private training and validation accuracy when learning rate and training duration/noise are retuned, while the training–validation gap increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under a fixed privacy budget with independently optimized training duration, larger batches can improve DP-SGD validation accuracy despite a larger generalization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Group normalization, weight standardization, augmentation multiplicity and parameter averaging improve the private training pipeline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: These architectural and training changes improve CIFAR-10 accuracy under the tested DP-SGD recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: One augmentation per example reduces accuracy, whereas sufficiently high augmentation multiplicity improves it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data augmentation's benefit in DP-SGD depends on averaging multiple augmentations before clipping each example's gradient.

record.problems: The main batch-size gap evidence is from a figure whose exact values are not stated in text. It uses validation accuracy and DP-SGD, not standard non-private test error. ImageNet experiments used a very limited hyperparameter sweep and a single random seed. The paper reports no dropout ablation numbers, only a textual statement.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows omitted. Figure-only quantitative values for the batch-size accuracy sweep were not reconstructed; the textually stated direction and gap change are retained in R1.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out accuracy compared with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond the point of zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

Held-out performance across batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets, and controlled recovery from an established large-batch penalty. Optimizing duration separately for each batch size does not test these comparisons.

Benefits in non-private training; dependence on training-set size and dropout strength; combined removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation. Dropout configurations, separate effect sizes and tuning coverage are not reported.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Accuracy after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Add a qualitative dropout comparison: the authors report reduced training and validation accuracy when using dropout in private CIFAR-10 training. Record numerical values, dropout settings and uncertainty as not stated; distinguish this from the accompanying weight-decay finding.
missing.locator: Section 3.1, Baseline model and private training pipeline for CIFAR-10

record.verdict_notes: V6 does not explicitly exclude private classifiers, so the authors' dropout finding is eligible evidence in a new regime. It qualifies scope rather than refuting the claim that suitably configured dropout helps in some regimes. No existing row measures dropout. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test-error behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning effects.
Non-private training; fixed epoch-budget comparisons; language models; effects of longer training, learning-rate warmup, normalization or regularization changes on the large-batch penalty.
Dropout effects in non-private classifiers and combined removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparison to norm- and margin-based measures.

rows.subject: WRN-16-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Batch-size sweep; training and validation accuracy measured across batch sizes 256 to 16384.
rows.measure: Training and validation accuracy; training–validation gap
rows.baseline: Batch size 256; exact accuracy values not stated
rows.value: Accuracy consistently improves as batch size rises; the training–validation gap also increases with batch size.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard error across 5 independent runs (figure caption); values not stated
rows.note: The paper reports higher accuracy with larger batches but explicitly notes a larger training–validation gap. It does not report a fixed-epoch comparison.
rows.check: Learning rate and training duration/noise are retuned for each batch size; optimal epochs increase for large batches. Validation accuracy improves, so the increasing training–validation gap cannot establish V5's fixed-epoch held-out penalty.

rows.subject: WRN-40-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Ablation adds group normalization to the baseline.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over 5 runs: validation (0.6); training (0.3)
rows.note: This is a normalization ablation, not a test of the version’s large-batch comparison.
rows.check: Group-normalization ablation at batch size 256, with no batch-size comparison. Table 2 reports medians and standard deviations.

rows.subject: WRN-40-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Ablation increases batch size from 256 to 4096.
rows.baseline: 50.8% validation accuracy; 51.2% training accuracy at batch size 256
rows.value: 70.0% validation accuracy; 73.4% training accuracy at batch size 4096
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over 5 runs: validation (0.6); training (0.9)
rows.note: Both accuracies rise, but training accuracy rises more; the paper’s separate gap statement concerns the WRN-16-4 batch-size sweep.
rows.check: The correct immediate baseline is 66.3% validation and 67.9% training accuracy with group normalization at batch size 256. Increasing the batch to 4096 gives 70.0% and 73.4%, respectively. Epoch budgets are optimized separately, so this does not test V5.

rows.subject: WRN-40-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Ablation adds weight standardization after group normalization and batch-size increase.
rows.baseline: 66.3% validation accuracy; 67.9% training accuracy after group normalization
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over 5 runs: validation (1.0); training (1.3)
rows.note: The ablation measures adding weight standardization, not a condition named in V5.
rows.check: The correct immediate baseline is 70.0% validation and 73.4% training accuracy at batch size 4096. Adding weight standardization gives 71.2% and 74.7%. This is not a controlled comparison of large- versus small-batch penalties.

rows.subject: WRN-40-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Adds augmentation multiplicity of 16 to the preceding ablation setup.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over 5 runs: validation (0.9); training (0.9)
rows.note: This ablation changes augmentation multiplicity, which is outside the conditions in V5.
rows.check: Measures augmentation multiplicity at one batch size, without establishing or measuring recovery from a large-batch penalty. It also does not manipulate dropout.

rows.subject: WRN-40-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Adds exponential moving average of parameters to the preceding ablation setup.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation over 5 runs: validation (0.2); training (0.2)
rows.note: This ablation changes parameter averaging, which is outside the conditions in V5.
rows.check: Measures parameter averaging at one batch size; no version names this comparison.

rows.subject: WRN-16-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Sweeps augmentation multiplicity from 1 to 32; multiplicity 1 is the ordinary augmentation comparison.
rows.value: Ordinary data augmentation reduced both training and validation accuracies; exact values figure only.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard error across 5 independent runs (figure caption)
rows.note: This tests data augmentation in DP-SGD, not dropout.
rows.check: Ordinary data augmentation reduces accuracy relative to no augmentation. This is not a dropout comparison and cannot be marked reversed for V6.

rows.subject: WRN-16-4
rows.stage_stated: trained with DP-SGD from random initialization
rows.baseline: No augmentation; exact accuracy values not stated
rows.value: Performance consistently improves with higher augmentation multiplicities, significantly exceeding performance without data augmentation.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard error across 5 independent runs (figure caption); values not stated
rows.note: This tests augmentation multiplicity, not dropout, and therefore is not direct evidence for V6’s dropout claim.
rows.check: Increasing augmentation multiplicity improves accuracy, but dropout is not manipulated. This cannot support V6.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 Wide-ResNet classifiers trained from random initialization with DP-SGD
relationships.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly reports that dropout reduced training and validation accuracy. This identifies an additional regime where dropout was detrimental; the evidence is textual and requires a missing row, with no reported configurations or effect sizes.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported lower training and validation accuracy without specifying dropout settings or effect sizes. This comparison has not been independently checked.
